source: Nairne (2002) The myth of the encoding-retrieval match
finding: Founding critique. Match between cue and trace is generally positive but correlational, not causal. Raising match can help, do nothing, or hurt. Predict retention from how diagnostic the cue is.
numbers: No experiment numbers in the abstract. Memory 10(5-6):389-395.
limits: Only the PubMed abstract was readable. Full text is paywalled (Taylor and Francis returned 403). The paper is an argument with a review of prior data, not a new experiment.
agent_relevance: Score keys by diagnostic value (target versus rivals), not by overlap with the query.

source: Higham (2002) Strong cues are not necessarily weak: Thomson and Tulving (1970) and the encoding specificity principle revisited
finding: Two-stage test splits free-report retrieval, forced-report retrieval, monitoring and report bias, applied to the original 1970 design. Cue reinstatement changed free-report recall, but with forced output the effect vanished.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract (the .26 versus .28 figures in K03 come from the earlier b-file, not re-checked here).
quote: once report bias and monitoring effects were removed by forcing output, retrieval was unaffected
limits: Abstract only. Human cued recall, not machine. Shows the strong-cue failure is a reporting artefact, not a retrieval one.
agent_relevance: When testing agent retrieval, measure forced and free report separately. Do not read a gated miss as a retrieval miss.

source: Tulving and Thomson (1973) Encoding specificity and retrieval processes in episodic memory
finding: NOT RETRIEVED. Journal page is paywalled and loads no text (APA PsycNet). Semantic Scholar lists it as closed access with 4751 citations. No founding numbers could be verified this session.
numbers: None verified.
limits: Recognition-failure percentages must not be cited from memory. Gap 2 stays open for this paper.
agent_relevance: None until the numbers are checked from a legal copy.

source: Watkins and Tulving (1975) Episodic memory: when recognition fails
finding: NOT RETRIEVED. A PubMed search for Watkins, Tulving, 1975 returned no record. The Wikipedia page on the principle does not mention it.
numbers: None verified.
limits: Gap 2 stays open for this paper. Postman (1975) is the only 1975 counter-study named by the Wikipedia page, with no numbers there.
agent_relevance: None until checked.

source: Badham, Poirier, Gandhi, Hadjivassiliou, Maylor (2016) Aging and memory as discrimination
finding: Exp 1 repeats Poirier et al. 2012 Exp 4 (RT, trained to high accuracy) with young and older adults. Exp 2 is a new paradigm scored on recall accuracy: word pairs on spot-the-difference images, unique versus shared (four-pair) backgrounds. Match helped only when the reinstated background was unique.
numbers: Exp 2: 30 young, 31 older. Unique beat shared at encoding F(1,59)=10.68, p=.002. Reinstating image at test F(1,59)=16.09, p<.001. Match benefit only with unique background t(60)=4.35, p<.001; shared background t<1. Match benefit larger in older adults F(1,59)=6.66, p=.012; not significant in young t(29)=1.60, p=.120. Exp 1 had 36 young and 36 older.
limits: Co-authored by Poirier, so not fully independent of the original lab. No preregistration mentioned in the text. Older adults show a match effect that the authors credit to fewer competitors, not to match itself. Young adults showed no reliable match benefit at all in Exp 2.
agent_relevance: Gives accuracy (not RT) support for: extra context helps only when it makes the cue unique. A session tag shared by many notes should not help.

source: Goh and Lu (2012) Testing the myth of the encoding-retrieval match
finding: Independent lab (National University of Singapore). Three experiments with word-pair cued recall. Diagnostic value of the cue predicted recall better than absolute encoding-retrieval match.
numbers: Three experiments; sample sizes and effect sizes not in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only this session. Badham et al. say Goh and Lu competitors were untrained (from the earlier critique). Preregistration not mentioned.
agent_relevance: Second lab, accuracy outcome, supports using diagnostic value as the key score.

source: Murre (2021) The Godden and Baddeley (1975) experiment on context-dependent memory on land and underwater: a replication
finding: Failed replication of the classic environmental context effect. Divers studied and recalled on land or underwater; same-context recall was not better.
numbers: N=16 divers, all four combinations within subject, 4-minute retention.
quote: we did not find that recall in the same context where the words had been learned was better
limits: Small sample. Recall delay only 4 minutes. The author lists design differences from the original.
agent_relevance: Supports the view that the plain context bonus is weak when other cues exist. Do not expect a large benefit from environment tags.

source: Koch and Coutanche (2024) Context reinstatement requires a schema relevant virtual environment to benefit object recall
finding: Virtual reality test of context-dependent memory. Same environment gave better object recall, but also more false recognition of similar lures. Benefit needed a schema-congruent object and environment and appeared for recall, not recognition.
limits: Abstract only. Benefit is conditional on congruence, which is a semantic link between context and item.
agent_relevance: A tag helps when it is meaningfully tied to the content, which fits the idea of distinctive, relevant keys. Tags can also raise false matches.

source: Isarida, Isarida, Sakai (2012) Effects of study time and meaningfulness on environmental context-dependent recognition
finding: Direct outshining test in humans. Place-context recognition effect appeared with short study time (1.5 s per item) but not with long study time (4.0 s). It still appeared for nonwords at long study time, which have no strong meaning cue.
numbers: Exp 1: 80 undergraduates. Exp 2: 40 undergraduates.
limits: Recognition test. Abstract only. Authors say results fit the outshining account.
agent_relevance: Fits outshining: context helps when the item has no strong own cue. For an agent: tags for notes that lack a strong semantic key.

source: Yuvruk (2026) Context brings back all the memories: a review of the physical context reinstatement effect on episodic memory
finding: Review of the outshining and ICE hypotheses. Reinstating study context seems to help when context is semantically rich, the item is unfamiliar, cue load is low, encoding was interactive, and the retention interval was long. Heterogeneous methods and response bias may explain conflicting results.
numbers: No pooled numbers in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Narrative review, not a new meta-analysis. Smith and Vela 2001 remains the only quantitative synthesis found (its abstract: reinstatement, and noncontextual cues at learning and at test, each reduce the context effect).
agent_relevance: Gives five conditions for when a tag may help. Low cue load and long interval map to: few rival notes and many intervening writes.

source: Hammond et al. (2019) No environmental context-dependent effect, but interference, of physical activity on object location memory
finding: Failed replication and extension: standing versus walking did not work as a context cue in two experiments. Walking lowered location memory instead. Authors point to the outshining hypothesis.
numbers: Two experiments; N not in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Another null for weak context cues when other cues exist.

source: Ensor, Surprenant, Neath, Hockley (2023) Using preexperimental familiarity to compare the ICE and cue-overload accounts of context-dependent memory in item recognition
finding: Three experiments. Results favoured the ICE account over cue overload and suggest context does not act as a retrieval cue in recognition.
numbers: N not in the abstract.
limits: Recognition only. Abstract only. Cuts against a pure cue-overload story for context effects.
agent_relevance: Warns that the machine analogy to cue overload may not hold for tag effects in recognition-like checks.

source: Antony and Bennion (2023) Semantic associates create retroactive interference on an independent spatial memory task
finding: Interference through semantic associates (indirect cue overload). It occurred in three experiments when the interfering items came shortly before the test, but not with a 1-hour delay before the test.
numbers: Three experiments; N not in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Interference, not tag benefit, was measured. A delay removed the effect here, the reverse of what a simple delay account predicts.
agent_relevance: Delay changes interference as well as cue benefit. Test both at several gaps.

source: Guo, Wu, Yiu (2026) The Interference Gap: Comparing Retrieval Bounds in Human Memory and RAG Systems (arXiv 2606.28327)
finding: Verified from the arXiv page and HTML. The abs page itself shows id 2606.28327 and Submitted 9 May 2026 (v1 only), so the oddity is on arXiv's own record, not a citation error; the page does not explain it. Human data come from Prolific, not preregistered. No data or code link found in the text. Human fan tested at 1, 2, 4 only; fan 8 is simulation only.
numbers: Prolific N=120, 8 excluded, N=112. Fan 1, 2, 4 with 40 persons and 40 locations; 60 study sentences, 120 recognition trials. RAG: 200 entities at each of fan 1, 2, 4, 8 (800 pairs per system). Slopes a/s: human .41, DPR .67, HippoRAG .44 (abstract).
limits: Preprint, one lab, no replication. Authors say the study was not preregistered and a follow-up is in preparation. Human task is recognition; RAG task is top-1 retrieval, so the matched paradigm is loose. Mechanism not separated.
agent_relevance: Use as a hint that human fan sensitivity is lower than dense retrieval, not as a result. No replication of the human slope exists.

source: Yang et al. (2026) RaMem: Contextual Reinstatement for Long-term Agentic Memory (arXiv 2606.22844)
finding: Closest direct test found. Session, time and participant context stored with each memory and used for ranking on LoCoMo and LongMemEval. A shuffle test keeps content and metadata length but moves the context fields across entries: wrong tags are worse than no tags.
numbers: Temporal-triggered subset, GPT-4.1-mini: ground-truth Recall@10 0.8066 full; 0.5708 without session context; 0.2358 with shuffled temporal context. Qwen3-8B: 0.7217 full, 0.4245 without, 0.1840 shuffled. All questions, GPT-4.1-mini: F1 0.5291 to 0.5004, GT R@10 0.7550 to 0.6744 under shuffle. Context-confusable subset: R@10 0.6842 to 0.7510 (GPT-4.1-mini). Overall Recall@10 0.7221 to 0.7890. Average F1 GPT-4o 39.06 to 51.66.
limits: Method adds several parts at once (condition induction, ranking, synthesis), so the tag effect is confounded. No same-length filler arm and no arm with a strong semantic key removed, so outshining is not tested. Gains are larger for time-cued questions. Preprint, one lab.
agent_relevance: Wrong tags hurt more than none. A tag must be bound to the right note. Time and session tags help when the query itself points to an episode.

source: Yousuf et al. (2026) Utilizing Metadata for Better Retrieval-Augmented Generation (arXiv 2601.11863)
finding: Metadata (company, year, form type, section) prefixed to SEC-filing chunks improves retrieval over plain chunks in highly repetitive text. Dropping company and year hurts most; dropping section titles hurts little.
numbers: General questions, k=5, text-embedding-3-small: Context@5 33.33 plain, 55.00 prefix, 48.33 suffix, 63.33 unified dual encoder. bge-m3: 26.67 plain, 61.67 prefix. Avg rank 21.61 to 10.22 (OpenAI).
limits: No filler-prefix control. Only 60 questions per type (steps of 1.67 points). Repetitive corpus where documents differ mainly by identifiers, so distinctive fields are close to the whole signal.
agent_relevance: In a store of near-duplicate notes, a distinguishing prefix field is worth the tokens. The field ablation shows the distinguishing identifiers carry the gain.

source: Yuan, Su, Yao (2026) Diagnosing Retrieval vs. Utilization Bottlenecks in LLM Agent Memory (ICLR 2026, arXiv 2603.02473)
finding: On LoCoMo, how memory is retrieved matters more than how it is written. Raw chunks with speaker names and timestamps equal or beat extracted facts and summaries. On conversational memory, plain cosine beats BM25 by 16 points.
numbers: 1,540 questions, k=5, GPT-5-mini reader, text-embedding-3-small. Accuracy by retrieval: cosine 73.4, BM25 57.1, hybrid pool plus GPT-5.2 rerank 77.2. Raw chunks: cosine 77.9, BM25 59.2, hybrid 81.1. Write strategy spread 3-8 points; retrieval spread 14-23. Retrieval precision vs accuracy r=0.98.
limits: No ratio rule, no IDF variant beyond BM25, no tag ablation. Hybrid adds an LLM reranker, so the gain is not from the scoring rule alone. One benchmark, one reader.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 partial: cosine, BM25 and hybrid compared on agent memory. Conversational paraphrase favours semantic over lexical. A rival-aware ratio score was not tested.

source: Cuconasu et al. (2024) The Power of Noise: Redefining Retrieval for RAG Systems (SIGIR 2024), full text re-read
finding: Random documents added to the prompt raised accuracy in several models. Authors give attention entropy as a possible reason (entropy 3 times higher with random documents) and say they cannot answer definitively.
numbers: Llama2-7b, MPT, Phi-2, Falcon; NQ-open; Wikipedia dump of Dec 2018. Gold only (Llama2): 0.5642; closed book 0.1123. +35% = +0.07 absolute, with 4 retrieved Contriever documents and random documents added up to the context limit. BM25 retrievers: +3-4 points. Random from Reddit and random-word sentences also helped. Best setup: 3-5 retrieved documents plus random fill.
quote: we cannot yet answer this question in a definitive manner
limits: 2024 small open models only. The +35% peak is on a weak base (about 0.2 accuracy). The gain depends on gold being present and on document position (random docs far from the query). No frontier model, and no replication on 2025-2026 models found.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on padding. The effect is unexplained and was not tested on current models. Treat it as noise that may change attention, not as a retrieval fact.

source: Wu et al. (2025, v4) Pandora's Box or Aladdin's Lamp: a comprehensive analysis revealing the role of RAG noise in LLMs
finding: Seven noise types in a multiple-choice RAG benchmark. Counterfactual noise hurts most. Semantic, datatype and illegal-sentence noise (URLs, junk text) added to the gold context raised accuracy a little. Authors link it to more attention on the gold context and higher confidence.
numbers: Llama3-8B-Instruct average over 7 sets: gold only 86.57; counterfactual 45.58 (-40.99); illegal sentence 89.89 (+3.32). Qwen2-7B: gold only 86.46; counterfactual 33.96 (-52.50); illegal sentence 88.11 (+1.65). Eight LLMs in total.
limits: Small 2024 models, multiple choice, gold document always present. Gains are 1.6-3.3 points, much smaller than the +35% peak. Mechanism from a hypothesis test, not an intervention.
agent_relevance: Second source for a small benefit of junk text when gold is present. Also shows that similar-but-wrong (counterfactual) text is by far the worst.

source: Gao, Chen, Huang (2026) The First Drop of Ink: nonlinear impact of distracting information in long-context reasoning (arXiv 2605.10828)
finding: Hard distractors (topically close, answer-free, BM25-retrieved) hurt sharply at small proportions, then plateau. Easy (filler sentence) and random Wikipedia passages are the neutral comparison. Theory: hard distractors get gold-like attention logits and take up the softmax denominator.
numbers: 128K contexts, 100 distractor documents: attention on the gold document 97% with 0% hard, 21% with 10% hard (76% fall). Models: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen3-Next-80B-Instruct; NQ, TriviaQA, PopQA, HotpotQA; 200 examples per setting. Filtering gains come mostly from shorter context, not from removal.
limits: Open models only; accuracy is string containment. The attention account is theory plus retrieval-head measurements. Does not add random documents on top of gold plus retrieved, so it does not test the Cuconasu effect.
agent_relevance: Softmax attention behaves like a ratio rule: gold weight over the sum of rivals. A few close rivals cost more than many unrelated notes. Keep near-duplicates out of the prompt.

source: Amiraz, Cuconasu, Filice, Karnin (2025) The Distracting Effect: Understanding Irrelevant Passages in RAG (arXiv 2505.06914)
finding: Defines a per-passage distracting effect that is stable across LLMs. Irrelevant passages from stronger retrievers distract more. Fine-tuning on hard distractors gave up to +7.5%. Cites Cuconasu 2024 for random passages not degrading answers.
numbers: Models include Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, Falcon-3-3B and 7B, Qwen-2.5-3B and 7B. Up to 7.5% higher accuracy from training on hard distractors.
limits: Fine-tuning result, not a prompt-only change. Does not re-test the +35% random-document effect.
agent_relevance: A better retriever makes its own mistakes more costly. Make the agent check retrieved notes, not trust rank.

source: Joren et al. (2025) Sufficient Context: a new lens on retrieval augmented generation systems (ICLR 2025, arXiv 2411.06037)
finding: Tests the Higham question in machines. Strong models do not withhold too much; they answer too often. Adding retrieved context lowered abstention on insufficient context. Models also answered correctly without sufficient context.
numbers: Abstention on insufficient context, without versus with RAG: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 84.1% to 52%; GPT-4o 34.4% to 31.2%; Gemini 1.5 Pro 100% to 18.6%. Over 35% correct with insufficient context on HotpotQA. 55.4% of instances in a standard dataset had insufficient context (MuSiQue example). Selective generation raises the correct fraction among answered by 2-10% for Gemini, GPT and Gemma.
limits: No forced-listing arm, so the Higham recovery test (how many correct candidates are withheld) is still missing. 2024 models. Abstention here is judged per question, not on an agent's candidate list.
agent_relevance: The direction differs from humans: report bias in LLMs is toward over-answering. Gating helps precision at some cost; the cost in lost correct answers is not reported.

source: Pham, Nguyen, Chen, Ye (2026) LongHarness Bench: stress-testing language model harnesses for long-context reasoning (arXiv 2609.38137)
finding: Tool-using harnesses (OpenCode, mini-swe-agent, RLM, ReAct with embedding search) on recent frontier models. Semantic search surfaces related items but does not chain evidence. No NoLiMa-style literal versus non-literal test.
numbers: Best model-harness pair 68% macro accuracy. Outlier Memo Detection: ReAct with embedding retrieval 6% ($2.77) versus direct inference 44% ($1.17). Equivalent Program Pair Search: direct 44% ($0.78) rises to 52% ($2.68) with an embedding shortlist. Models named: GPT-5.6-sol, Gemini 3.8 Flash, GLM-5.3, Qwen3.8-27B, Kimi-K2.6.
limits: Does not manipulate word overlap between query and target, so Gap 8 is not answered. Model names are as printed in the paper.
agent_relevance: Retrieval by similarity alone is not enough for linked facts. Combine lexical lookup, semantic lookup and reading.

source: Wu et al. (2026) LongMemEval-V2: evaluating long-term agent memory toward experienced colleagues (arXiv 2605.12493), abstract only
finding: Agent memory benchmark with up to 500 trajectories and 115M tokens. A coding agent that stores trajectories as files and searches them beat the best RAG baseline.
numbers: AgentRunbook-C 72.5% average accuracy; strongest RAG baseline 48.5%; off-the-shelf coding agent 69.3%. 451 questions.
limits: Only the abstract and header were read. No literal-match manipulation, so it does not answer Gap 8. Latency cost is high.
agent_relevance: Evidence that file or tool search can outperform one-shot embedding retrieval in an external store.

source: Wang and Sun (2025) Unable to Forget: proactive interference reveals working memory limits in LLMs beyond context length (PI-LLM, arXiv 2506.08184)
finding: Streams related key-value updates and queries the final values. Accuracy falls log-linearly toward zero as the number of earlier values for a key grows, even when the final value sits next to the query. Telling the model to ignore earlier input helped little.
numbers: Log-linear decline across models; exact slopes not extracted this session.
quote: LLM retrieval accuracy declines log-linearly toward zero as interference accumulates
limits: Same-key overwrites, not a tag manipulation. It measures how interference grows with intervening writes, not how a tag benefit grows.
agent_relevance: Supports the delay worry for Gap 10: more intervening writes to similar keys hurts. A tag must separate old and new values.

source: Roberts, Moore, Pham, Ewaleifoh, Fisher (2024) Large language model recall uncertainty is modulated by the fan effect (arXiv 2407.06349)
finding: Fan effect appears in token-probability uncertainty, not in reaction time. Present in some models only (Mistral, SOLAR); disappears when uncertainty is removed. A separate line of evidence for fan-like cost in LLMs, earlier than Guo et al.
numbers: No accuracy slopes in the part read.
limits: Model-dependent; uncertainty measure, not accuracy. Only some models show it.
agent_relevance: Fan cost in machines is partly model-specific. Do not assume a universal slope.

source: Poirier, Nairne, Morin, Zimmermann, Koutmeridou, Fowler (2012) Memory as discrimination: a challenge to the encoding-retrieval match principle
finding: Four experiments, cued recognition with 3-4 targets per set. Raising encoding-retrieval match could help, do nothing or hurt, depending on whether the added cue stayed diagnostic. Main measure was response time, with learning trained to high accuracy.
numbers: Exp 1, 2, 4: 4 targets with trios of cues; Exp 3: 3 targets with cue pairs. Sample sizes not in the abstract (earlier files give 21-25).
quote: increasing the encoding-retrieval match can hinder performance
limits: Abstract only here. Reaction time at near-ceiling accuracy; same lab as Nairne. Later work by Goh and Lu 2012 and Badham et al. 2016 used recall accuracy. A PubMed search for 'memory as discrimination' returned one paper and no preregistered replication was found.
agent_relevance: The cleanest human demonstration that more overlap can hurt when it adds rivals.

source: Wu et al. (2025) LongMemEval: Benchmarking chat assistants on long-term interactive memory (ICLR 2025), key-design study
finding: Closest direct test of Gap 1 and Gap 3 on agent memory. Index key is the stored text alone, a condensed form alone (extracted fact, summary, keyphrase), or the stored text plus the condensed form. Condensed keys alone lose to the plain text key. Text plus extracted user facts wins. A keyphrase added to a round-level key hurt. This is the match-times-distinctiveness picture: a distinct tag alone loses the match, a tag added to the match helps.
numbers: LongMemEval_M, Table 3. Value=round, Recall@10: K=V .692; K=fact .654; K=keyphrase .392; K=V+fact .784; K=V+keyphrase .636. Value=session, Recall@10: K=V .783; K=summary .648; K=fact .814; K=keyphrase .576; K=V+summary .749; K=V+fact .862; K=V+keyphrase .768. End-to-end GPT-4o Top-10 accuracy, round: .670 (K=V) vs .720 (V+fact). Paper summary: +9.4 percent recall@k and +5.4 percent accuracy on average across models for V+fact.
quote: using these condensed forms alone does not enhance the memory recall performance
limits: No filler arm: V+fact adds tokens to the key, so part of the gain may be extra text. Facts are LLM-extracted content, not a scene or context line. Session K=fact Recall@10 .814 beat K=V .783 but end-to-end Top-10 accuracy for GPT-4o fell (.512 vs .676). One run per cell, no confidence intervals.
agent_relevance: Do not replace the raw note by a short distinctive key. Append the distinctive line to the raw note to form the key, and test it against a same-length neutral line.

source: Wu et al. (2025) LongMemEval, appendix E.2 and E.3: three retrievers and rank merging vs key merging
finding: The gain from a distinctive extra key depends on how weak the plain key already is. Fact expansion helps most for the lexical retriever (BM25), least for the strongest dense retriever, and turns slightly negative at round level with Stella. Keeping the extra key in a separate index and merging ranks was clearly worse than merging text into one key. A partial outshining pattern: the tag helps most where the plain cue is weakest.
numbers: Table 9, Recall@5, value=session: BM25 .634 to .683 with fact (+.049); Contriever .723 to .762 (+.039); Stella V5 1.5B .720 to .732 (+.012). Value=round: BM25 .472 to .554 (+.082); Contriever .589 to .612 (+.023); Stella .660 to .644 (-.016). Summary expansion, session: BM25 .634 to .626, Contriever .723 to .732, Stella .720 to .689 (-.031). Table 10: rank merging scored below key merging; authors suggest the (m+1) times larger index as a reason.
limits: Retriever strength is confounded with model family and training data. One run per cell; differences of .01 to .02 are within noise. Not a crossed design of tag type by strong-key present or absent.
agent_relevance: Test distinctive tags on the weakest retriever first and expect the biggest gain there. With a strong dense retriever, extra tags may add nothing or hurt.

source: Wu et al. (2025) LongMemEval, history length and time-aware indexing (Table 1b, Table 4)
finding: Gap 7, partial. More intervening history lowers accuracy sharply even though the answer is present (oracle sessions vs the 115k-token history). A date tag used as an index key and query filter raised recall most when the value was a short round and a fact key was also present, and only with a strong model extracting the time range.
numbers: Table 1b, no chain-of-note, oracle vs S: GPT-4o .870 to .606 (30.3 percent drop); Llama 3.1 70B .710 to .454 (36.1 percent); Llama 3.1 8B .660 to .342 (48.1 percent). Table 4 temporal subset, value=round, K=V+fact, Recall@10: .550 plain; .722 with GPT-4o time-range query expansion; .570 with Llama 3.1 8B expansion. Value=session Recall@10: .721 to .797 (GPT-4o). Text: average gain 11.3 percent (round) and 6.8 percent (session).
limits: The tag is a date, not a free-text distinguishing line. Rows for Phi-3 models in Table 1b were not read reliably from the PDF layout and are omitted. History length and number of same-key writes are not separated.
agent_relevance: Tag benefit versus number of intervening writes was not measured. What is known: accuracy falls steeply as history grows, and a precise structured tag with a strong extractor recovers part of it.

source: Li et al. (2026) Locomo-Plus: beyond-factual cognitive memory evaluation framework for LLM agents
finding: A direct machine analogue of encoding-retrieval mismatch. Each test has a cue stated earlier and a later trigger query that is semantically disconnected from it. Every method collapses relative to factual LoCoMo, embedding retrieval is the weakest, and memory systems that rewrite or structure memories (Mem0, A-Mem, SeCom) do not escape the gap.
limits: LoCoMo-Plus is scored by a constraint-consistency judge and LoCoMo by string metrics, so the gap column mixes metrics. Cue-trigger pairs are LLM-generated with human filtering. No test of write-time tags or multiple keys. One run per system.
agent_relevance: When the later need does not resemble the stored wording, plain embedding on the raw text fails. Store a second intent-level key (what this note will matter for) and test it on disconnected triggers.

source: Neeser, Latimer, Khatri, Latimer, Ramakrishnan (2025) QuOTE: Question-Oriented Text Embeddings
finding: Gap 6 direct test: store hypothetical questions that a chunk can answer beside the chunk. Gains grow with the number of similar competing chunks, which is the cue-overload logic. HyDE (query-side hypothetical answer) did not help on SQuAD and cost about 10 times more per query.
numbers: Context accuracy top-1 / top-5: SQuAD naive 79.31 / 95.88; HyDE 76.60 / 92.63; QuOTE 90.03 / 98.48 (index time 10.36 s vs 170.32 s). Natural Questions naive 32.92 / 89.23; HyDE 33.23 / 90.46; QuOTE 38.00 / 92.15. MultiHop-RAG full match at 5 / 20 docs: naive 7.00 / 23.00; HyDE 6.00 / 23.50; QuOTE 8.00 / 29.00. Relative gain on SQuAD rose from about 8 percent with few contexts to over 20 percent with many; NQ 6 to 18.3 percent. Diminishing returns beyond about 10 to 15 questions per chunk.
limits: Question text is both a distinct key and extra tokens; no length-matched neutral control. MultiHop-RAG gains are small in absolute terms. SQuAD probes are extractive questions, which favours question-shaped keys. 2024-class models.
agent_relevance: Supports the question-shaped key direction (Fisher 1979, Gap 6) and the point that the value of a distinct key grows with competitor density. Still needs a test on agent notes with non-extractive later queries.

source: Gospodinov, MacAvaney, Macdonald (2023) Doc2Query--: when less is more
finding: Doc2Query writes extra queries per document and indexes them. Many generated queries are hallucinated and hurt. Filtering them with a relevance model improved retrieval, cut the index by about a third and sped up queries. Distinctive added keys help only if they stay true to the item.
numbers: MS MARCO dev RR@10: BM25 .185; Doc2Query (n=40) .277; with ELECTRA filter (30 percent dropped) .316; MonoT5 filter (40 percent) .308; TCT filter (50 percent) .287 (filters significant vs unfiltered). TREC DL'19 nDCG@10 .626 to .667. Mean response time 30 ms to 23 ms; index 1.17 GB to 0.89 GB. Abstract: up to 16 percent better.
limits: Seq2seq generator (T5) on web passages, not agent notes. The filter is a trained relevance model.
agent_relevance: If the agent writes tags or questions at write time, check that each is supported by the note. A wrong tag is worse than none (compare K19).

source: Zhou, Huang et al. (2025) Do retrieval augmented language models know when they do not know?
finding: Gap 5, the opposite risk to Higham's report bias. When all retrieved chunks are irrelevant, retrieval-augmented models refuse questions they can answer unaided (over-refusal). One positive chunk markedly reduces refusal. Refusal tuning (R-tuning) increases over-refusal. Under bad context models withhold; under good context they do not.
numbers: Table 3 (column labels as printed: no context, 0p10n, 10p0n, 1p9n): vanilla .579 / .191 / .759 / .738; R-tuning .444 / .138 / .750 / .682; ICFT(n) .734 / .632 / .750 / .591; ICFT(p) .750 / .658 / .824 / .723. Qwen-2.5-7B and LLaMA-3.1-8B on RGB English and Chinese. Text: over-refusal rises in the all-negative setting for every knowledge type.
limits: 7-8B open models, not frontier. The precise metric behind Table 3 was not fully resolved from the PDF text; use the trend only. Not a forced-listing test in Higham's design.
agent_relevance: Confidence gating can withhold in both directions. Test forced listing of top candidates before gating, and report over-answering and over-withholding separately.

source: Itai et al. (2026) LIT-RAGBench: benchmarking generator capabilities of LLMs in RAG (LREC 2026)
finding: Measured over-abstention (declining although evidence suffices) for 15 recent models. Rates vary widely; Claude-Sonnet-4 over-abstains most. Many models also fabricate answers when evidence is truly insufficient. Both error types exist in the same models.
numbers: 114 questions (Japanese; English by machine translation with human curation). Over-abstention ja / en / avg: Claude-Sonnet-4 .148 / .370 / .259; Llama-3.1-8B .204 / .222 / .213; Llama-3.3-70B .093 / .222 / .157; Gemma-3-27B .120 avg; GPT-4.1 .083; GPT-5 .065; Gemini-2.5-Pro .000 / .093 / .046; o3 .046; GPT-4.1 mini .028. No model above 90 percent overall.
limits: Small question set (rates move in steps of about 1/54), LLM judge, fictional entities. Shuffled table chunks drove some abstentions.
agent_relevance: Update to K22: LLMs both under- and over-abstain depending on model and context quality. The Higham-type check (what does forced listing recover?) is still unrun.

source: Hanley (1984) Dual processes in recognition and in recognition failure (Memory and Cognition 12, 575-580)
finding: Gap 10 partial. Open secondary account of the recognition-failure paradigm and the Tulving-Wiseman function. Reads recognition failure as a probabilistic mix of items recognised by familiarity of the target alone and items recognised through contextual retrieval (implicit backward recall of the list cue). Deviations from the function arise when instructions change cue-target integration. Fisher 1979 Exp 1 is read as support for backward recall.
numbers: No new data. Cites Tulving and Thomson (1973) and Watkins and Tulving (1975) only as the origin of the effect and Tulving and Wiseman (1975) for the function. It gives no 1973 or 1975 percentages.
limits: Theory note. The 1973 and 1975 figures asked for in Gap 10 were not reached: the journal pages are paywalled, and the Wikipedia page for the phenomenon (also opened) has no figures.
agent_relevance: Cue-to-target and target-to-cue routes can differ. For an agent store, test both lookup directions (from the cue to the note, and from the note back to its key) before trusting one.
